summary: Root cause: auth-service (SEV-2, INC-008) was saturated by a ~3.9x external login-demand surge that outgrew its fixed capacity — no code or config regression occurred. Starting in the 06:50Z bucket, offered login demand through api-gateway stepped up ~3.9x (auth-service ~395 -> ~1470-1538 req/s), coincident to the bucket with p99 rising from ~90ms to ~3.8s and CPU pinning to ~96-98%; the 64-thread worker pool hit 64/64 with accept-queue backlog up to ~98k, the autoscaler wanted 14 replicas but was capped at maxReplicas=8, and app-level admission control began rejecting connections with 'accept queue full' 503s at 06:55:42Z. The reporter's bcrypt-regression theory (HIST-101) is not reproduced: deployment sweeps covering 01:00-09:00Z found no auth-service release, and the only config change anywhere was a 03:40Z log-verbosity edit ~3h10m pre-onset. The gateway is a demonstrated unsaturated pass-through, and the shared redis-cache dependency was eliminated by direct measurement (hit-ratio flat/locally high, evictions and clients flat, CPU ~21-23% while auth pinned ~96%, zero WARN+ logs). Confidence in the top hypothesis is medium (0.70), capped by the unresolvable per-route attribution detail. Fix direction: relieve/raise auth-service capacity and throttle or absorb the external login demand — not an auth-service rollback.

ranked_hypotheses.title: External login demand surge outgrew auth-service capacity (no change required)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Starting in the 06:50Z bucket, offered login demand through api-gateway steps up ~3.9x (auth-service ~395 -> ~1470-1513 req/s). auth-service is provisioned for ~400 req/s with a fixed 64-thread worker pool and maxReplicas=8; it saturates (pool 64/64, accept-queue backlog ~98k, autoscaler wants 14 but is capped at 8), CPU pins to ~96-98%, tail latency inflates to ~3.8s, and the app's own admission control rejects connections with 'accept queue full' 503s from 06:55:42Z. No deployment or config change coincides with onset, so the origin is auth-service capacity being outgrown by offered load, not a code or config regression. The upstream generator of the demand (external traffic event, retry storm, client bug) is unidentified and is not a service-level fault in the inspected graph.

causal_chain.claim: Offered login demand steps up ~3.9x in the 06:50Z bucket, coincident to the second with the degradation onset (baseline ~380-405 -> 680 -> ~1450-1538 req/s).

The demand enters through api-gateway, whose request_rate steps up in the same 06:50Z bucket (~1228 -> ~4790-4991 req/s) while the gateway itself stays unsaturated (CPU ~40-44%, memory flat ~56-62%, restarts 0, zero ERROR logs).

auth-service hydration: fixed worker pool (64/64 threads, queue depths to 98763) plus maxReplicas=8 caps the service so it cannot absorb the load; autoscaler wants 14 replicas and cannot scale further.
CPU pins to ~96-98% (from ~38%) with memory flat ~51-53%, confirming compute-bound saturation rather than a memory leak or I/O wait.
Queued requests inflate the tail: p99 goes 88-92ms -> ~3.8s.

Worker-pool saturation drives the app's own admission control ('request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)'), raising 5xx to ~14% from 06:55:42Z; rate_limited_per_min steps ~450x to ~870-943/min.

The gateway's own error_rate (06:54Z) and p99 (~3.8-4.2s, 06:54Z) lag its request-rate step (06:50Z) by one bucket and mirror auth-service p99, i.e. the gateway inherits degradation from the saturated downstream rather than originating it.
No deployment or config change falls in the immediate pre-onset interval or anywhere in the covered 01:00-09:00Z record touching the login path, so load — not a change — is the trigger.

assumptions: The ~3.9x request_rate increase is genuine offered load reaching auth-service (not a metric artifact or duplicate counting).

auth-service is the origin of its own saturation; it was not itself merely waiting on a stalled downstream (the app-level 'accept queue full' signature with CPU pinned argues against dependency wait, but is not strictly conclusive).
The upstream generator of the demand spike (external traffic event, retry storm, client bug) is unidentified; it is not a change-recorded service fault.
The unmeasured login-route multiplier is comparable to the auth-service aggregate multiplier (~3.8x), so the surge genuinely reaches the login path rather than being dominated by other auth routes.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Reintroduced bcrypt-cost regression on auth-service (reporter's theory)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: An auth-service code change raised the bcrypt work factor (as in HIST-101), making the login path CPU-bound and pinning auth-service CPU to ~97%, inflating p99 to ~4s and producing 503s. This would require an auth-service release or a sub-bucket config change raising hashing cost near onset; the fix would be to find and roll back that auth-service release.

causal_chain.claim: A release or sub-bucket config change raising bcrypt cost factor makes each login CPU-bound; aggregate CPU pins near 100% with flat memory.
CPU-bound hashing inflates per-request latency to ~4s on the login path.
Saturated CPU/worker threads produce 503s on /v1/auth/login.

assumptions: An auth-service release raising bcrypt cost exists but was missed by deployment queries (e.g. outside the covered windows, or a sub-bucket config change invisible to bucket-level sweeps).
The ~3.9x request-rate increase is a consequence (retries) rather than the cause — directly contrary to the observed coincident 06:50Z onset of load and latency.

ranked_hypotheses.title: External kyc-provider stall on the login path
ranked_hypotheses.statement: auth-service->kyc-provider (external, has_telemetry:false) stalls on the login path; blocked requests hold worker threads, saturating the 64-thread pool, inflating p99 and triggering 503s.

causal_chain.claim: kyc-provider becomes slow or unavailable.
auth-service login requests block waiting on the external call, exhausting the process-wide worker pool.
Pool saturation causes accept-queue-full 503s and elevated p99.

assumptions: kyc-provider is on the critical login path and degraded at onset (no telemetry available to verify).
A dependency-blocked pool would still present CPU pinned at ~97% — implausible for I/O wait, and the rejection is 'accept queue full', not an upstream timeout, which weakens this hypothesis.

ranked_hypotheses.title: api-gateway as the fault origin for the demand surge (collapsed into H1)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Originally proposed that a ~3.9x demand surge originates at api-gateway and auth-service saturation is collateral, implying a different fix (rate-limit/quota the gateway). Round-2 evidence shows the gateway is an unsaturated pass-through (CPU ~40-44%, memory flat, restarts 0, zero ERROR logs) whose error_rate and p99 LAG its own request-rate step by one bucket and mirror auth-service. The gateway is therefore not a distinct origin: it is the conduit for the same external offered load that saturates auth-service, yielding the same fix direction as H1. Collapsed into H1 to avoid double-counting one origin.

causal_chain.claim: api-gateway request_rate steps up at 06:50Z from ~1228 to a ~4790-4991 req/s plateau (~3.9x).
The gateway is NOT resource-bound: CPU flat ~40-44%, memory flat ~56-62%, restarts 0, zero ERROR logs.
The added gateway demand is passed downstream; auth-service request_rate rises ~3.9x in the same bucket, saturating its worker pool.
The gateway's own 5xx and p99 rises (both 06:54Z) lag its request step (06:50Z) and mirror auth-service, a pass-through signature rather than a gateway self-fault.

assumptions: The gateway's request_rate is dominated by login-route traffic, or the added volume is offered external demand rather than internal fan-out from other services.
The ~3.2x gap between gateway added load (~3.6k req/s) and auth-service added load (~1.1k req/s) is unresolved and could include non-login or internal traffic.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Not a distinct origin from H1. The gateway is demonstrably an unsaturated pass-through: CPU flat ~40-44%, memory flat ~56-62%, restarts 0, zero ERROR logs (F27, F29), and its own error_rate and p99 step one bucket AFTER its request-rate step and mirror auth-service's values (F26, F28). Other gateway upstreams were flat across 06:40-07:10Z (F37), and the gateway and auth-service multipliers match within noise (F38), so the gateway does not originate the degradation — it conveys the same external offered load that saturates auth-service. Keeping it as a separate origin would double-count one root cause and misdirect the fix.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache cold-cache/miss storm or shared-node degradation stalls login
ranked_hypotheses.statement: redis-cache is the only shared dependency on the auth login path. A redis-side event (failover promoting an empty replica as in HIST-107, eviction/memory pressure, or co-tenant contention) causes a cache-miss storm / added latency per login, inflating auth-service p99 to ~4s and causing 503s.

causal_chain.claim: redis-cache experiences a failover/empty-replica or memory-pressure/eviction event.
A cache-miss storm or added per-call latency on the login path raises auth-service response times.
auth-service latencies rise and it eventually sheds load with 503s.

assumptions: Any sub-millisecond cache-side slowdown would be invisible because redis exposes no latency metric (F22).
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Rejected by direct measurement: redis hit_ratio_pct was flat and locally HIGH at 06:51Z (~94.4-97.4), not a collapse (F18); evictions_per_min showed no spike, 06:51Z within baseline (F19); connected_clients flat ~283-337 with no reconnect/replica-loss pattern (F20); redis cpu_pct low and flat ~20.6-25.6%, a local low at 06:51Z while auth-service CPU pinned ~96% (F21); and redis logged ZERO WARN-or-worse events across 06:30-07:20Z, ruling out restart/failover/replica-sync (F23). The reported 503 is app-level 'accept queue full' on a CPU-pinned, non-IO-wait service (F3, F5), and redis is not the bottleneck. HIST-107's cold-cache scenario is not reproduced.

facts.statement: auth-service p99 latency was flat ~88-92ms through 06:45Z, then jumped in the 06:50Z bucket (avg 844ms, max 3849ms) and sustained ~3.7-3.9s from 06:55Z through 08:55Z — onset ~15 min before the 07:06Z report.
auth-service error_rate was ~0.2% baseline until the 06:50Z bucket then jumped to 14.02% at 06:55Z and held ~13.6-14.3% through 08:55Z; the 5xx onset lags the latency jump by one bucket.

All 372 ERROR logs on auth-service share one signature: 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)', first seen 06:55:42Z — app-level admission control, not an upstream timeout or connection refused.

WARN logs show the causal chain before the first 503: 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=...)' first at 06:54:53Z with queue depths up to 98763, plus 'autoscaler: desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' from 06:57:15Z.
auth-service CPU was flat ~37-40% until the 06:50Z bucket then pinned ~96-98% through 08:55Z, while memory_pct stayed flat ~51-53% (CPU saturation with exhausted worker threads, not a memory leak).

Only one deployment occurred across all services near onset: portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803) at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z by ci-bot ('CSV export endpoint', status live, rolled_back_at null). No auth-service deployment appears.

Config changes 05:30-07:10Z across all services: zero. Widening to 00:00-07:10Z yields exactly one: cfg-2801 on auth-service, key log.level, INFO->WARN at 03:40:00Z by config-bot ('Reduce log volume') — a logging verbosity change ~2h50m before onset.

auth-service dependency edges are auth-service->user-db (db), auth-service->redis-cache (cache, shared:true), auth-service->kyc-provider (external, has_telemetry:false), and api-gateway->auth-service (http); no session-store or DNS/network node appears in the graph.
redis-cache is shared: auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service all write to it; user-db is NOT shared (only consumer edge is auth-service->user-db).

HIST-101 (2025-08-14, 'Login latency after auth-service release') has the same symptoms as INC-008 (login p99 4s, 503 on login, high cpu) with confirmed root cause 'bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0' (bad_deployment, rolled back); unlike INC-008 it was triggered by an auth-service release.

Widening the deployment check to 04:00-09:00Z still returns exactly one deployment across all services — portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 05:50:00Z, status live — with no auth-service deployment near the 06:50Z onset.
Config-change sweep over 04:00-09:00Z returned zero entries for all services; no feature flag, rate limit, pool size or timeout change precedes or coincides with onset.
redis-cache hit_ratio_pct was flat and locally HIGH at onset (06:51Z 96.48, oscillating 94.44-97.4, missing_points 0) — no cold-cache/miss-storm signature.
redis-cache evictions_per_min showed no eviction or memory-pressure event at onset (~2.4-3.7/min across 06:30-07:20Z; 06:51Z 2.86 within baseline).
redis-cache connected_clients was flat ~283-337 throughout onset with no reconnect/replica-loss pattern that a failover/empty-replica event (HIST-107) would produce.
redis-cache cpu_pct was flat and low ~20.6-25.6% (06:51Z a local low of 21.21) while auth-service CPU pinned at ~96% — the cache was not the bottleneck.
redis-cache exposes no latency metric and no request_rate/keyspace/key-count metric; only connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct are available.
redis-cache produced ZERO WARN-or-worse logs in 06:30-07:20Z (log data range 03:00-08:59Z) — no restart, failover, reconnect, or replica-sync warning recorded.

api-gateway request_rate was flat ~1220-1290 req/s through 06:48Z, rose in the 06:50Z bucket (avg 1500.82), climbed to avg 4790.49 (max 4859.74) by 06:58Z and held ~4660-4990 req/s through 07:10Z — same bucket as the auth-service latency/CPU onset.
The gateway request_rate increase is ~3.9x over a pre-onset level that was already ~1230 req/s, i.e. a further multiplier on an already-elevated baseline.

api-gateway error_rate was baseline ~0.13-0.31% through the 06:50-06:52Z buckets, then jumped at 06:54Z (avg 4.78/max 9.4) and held ~8.66-9.32% — one bucket AFTER its own request-rate jump and the auth-service latency jump, matching downstream 503 exposure.
api-gateway showed no resource saturation of its own: cpu_pct flat ~40-44% and memory_pct flat ~56-62% across 06:30-07:30Z, absorbing the ~3.9x traffic increase without CPU or memory pressure.

api-gateway latency_p99_ms was flat ~206-219ms through the 06:50Z bucket, then jumped at 06:54Z (avg 3952.31, max 4200.87) and stayed ~3816-4053ms — mirroring the auth-service login p99 (~3.8s) and lagging its own request-rate step by a bucket.
api-gateway logged ZERO ERROR entries in 06:30-07:30Z and its restarts count was 0 for the whole 06:30-07:09Z period — no gateway-local error signature or crash.
Deployment retry over 01:00-05:30Z succeeded and returned count=0 across all services, closing the last deployment-coverage hole under the deployment-regression hypotheses.

Config/flag changes over 01:00-05:30Z returned exactly one entry, not on the login path: cfg-2801 on auth-service, log.level INFO->WARN at 03:40:00Z — confirming no pool-size, timeout, rate-limit or feature-flag change to the login path.

Combined deployment/config record across 01:00-09:00Z is continuous and contains no auth-service release and no change to user-db, redis-cache, or any auth login-path component; the HIST-101 bcrypt-cost trigger is not reproduced in any window.
api-gateway exposes no per-route/by-path dimension: only aggregate gauges cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts.
The gateway produced ZERO log entries matching auth/login in 06:40-07:10Z, so no route-level attribution can be recovered from gateway logs.

Proxy attribution by upstream: gateway request_rate rose 1227.99 (06:48Z) to ~4790-4991 req/s (06:58-07:10Z) while the only upstream with a comparable surge was auth-service (386.14 -> 1749.75 -> 1469.29).
Other gateway upstreams were flat across 06:40-07:10Z (portfolio-service 559.17 -> 560.88; pricing-engine 640.15 -> 619.94; market-data-service 935.75 -> 967.77), contributing ~0 to the step-up.

auth-service rate_limited_per_min shows the same 06:54Z step as the login-route surge: baseline ~1.2-2.2/min through 06:52Z then 451.86 avg (max 902.06) at 06:54Z and ~870-943/min through 07:10Z — a ~450x increase in admission-rejected login requests.

auth-service metrics expose no route/path dimension (available_metrics = cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, rate_limited_per_min, request_rate, restarts), so p99/503 elevation cannot be split by route from metrics.

The only route-identifying telemetry is auth-service logs; in the ERROR stream every signature is on the login path ('request rejected: accept queue full, returning <n> (POST /v<n>/auth/login)'), 104 matches spanning 06:55:42Z-07:29:59Z, with no verify/refresh/token route appearing.

The WARN saturation stream is route-agnostic: 'worker pool saturated (active=<n>/<n>, queue=<n>)', 32 WARN entries with active=64/64 and queue depths 39035, 98763, 62284, first at 06:54:53Z; the pool is a single process-wide 64-thread pool shared by all routes.

Aggregate auth-service signals all step at the same 06:49-06:54Z bucket: latency_p99_ms 91.36 -> 3752.4; error_rate 0.19 -> 11.72 then ~13.7-14.2%; request_rate 395.18 -> 1512.39 (~3.8x); rate_limited_per_min ~1.8 -> 886.18 — a whole-service step, not route-partitioned.

assumptions: The ~3.9x request_rate increase is genuine offered load reaching auth-service, not a metric artifact or duplicate counting (supported by coincident CPU, queue-depth and rate-limit counters, but not independently metered per route).

auth-service is the origin of its own saturation and was not itself merely waiting on a stalled downstream; the app-level 'accept queue full' signature with CPU pinned argues against dependency wait, but is not strictly conclusive.
The upstream generator of the demand spike (external traffic event, retry storm, client bug) is unidentified and is not a change-recorded service fault.
The unmeasured login-route multiplier is comparable to the auth-service aggregate multiplier (~3.8x), so the surge genuinely reaches the login path rather than being dominated by other auth routes.

The ~3.2x absolute gateway (added ~3.6k req/s) vs auth-service (added ~1.1k req/s) delta is a composition artifact of a per-service proxy conflating route with upstream service, and does not indicate a different origin.
No sub-minute config change occurred inside the 06:50Z bucket at finer granularity than the bucket-level sweeps; only bucket-level correlation is available.
The 00:00-01:00Z sub-window has no deployment sweep, but at >5h before onset it is not a plausible immediate trigger.
The auth-service ERROR log stream sample (truncated at 104 matched / 40 returned) is representative, so /v1/auth/verify and /v1/auth/refresh are assumed to contribute no significant errors.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) auth-service request_rate was steady ~380-405 req/s from 05:00-06:45Z, jumped to 680.57 (max 1012) in the 06:50Z bucket and ~1450-1538 req/s (max 1813) from 06:55Z on — roughly 3.9x, coincident with the CPU/latency onset.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) No change in the window touches the login path: the sole deployment (portfolio-service 'CSV export endpoint') shares no dependency edge with auth-service except the platform node redis-cache.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) Change correlation is negative: latest deployable change before onset is the 03:40Z auth-service log.level config change (~3h10m before 06:50Z) and the 05:50Z portfolio-service deploy (~1h before); nothing falls in the 06:30-06:50Z pre-onset interval.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) Only one change of any kind exists in 01:00-05:30Z (the 03:40Z log.level edit, ~3h10m pre-onset); the latest deployable change anywhere is the 05:50Z portfolio-service deploy — neither touches auth-service or the login path.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) Multiplier attribution: the gateway rose ~4.1x (1227.99 -> 4990.58) while auth-service rose ~3.8x (386.14 -> 1469.29) — matching within measurement noise, consistent with a genuine login-demand surge.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) Because saturation is expressed at the shared process-wide resource layer (worker pool 64/64 with large accept-queue backlog, aggregate CPU/request-rate/rate-limit stepping together), the degradation mechanism is inherently route-agnostic; login is the dominant/first-hit path, consistent with all-route capacity exhaustion and not providing the login-only isolation a per-request bcrypt change would require.

timeline.event: Only change anywhere in the covered pre-onset period: cfg-2801 on auth-service, log.level INFO->WARN ('Reduce log volume'); a logging-verbosity change ~3h10m before onset, not on the login path.
Sole deployment across all services: portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803, 'CSV export endpoint', status live, not rolled back). Unrelated to auth/login path.
Last pre-onset sample: auth-service request_rate 395.18 req/s, p99 91.36ms, error_rate 0.19%, CPU ~37-40%; api-gateway request_rate 1227.99 req/s, p99 ~206-219ms, CPU ~40-44%.

Onset bucket: auth-service request_rate steps to 680.57 (max 1012) and p99 jumps to avg 844ms / max 3849ms; CPU steps to avg 71.88 / max 96.96. api-gateway request_rate begins rising (avg 1500.82, max 1652.95) in the same bucket.

redis-cache measured at onset with no anomaly: hit_ratio 96.48 (a local high), evictions 2.86/min, connected_clients 310.88, cpu_pct 21.21 (local low) while auth-service CPU pinned — shared cache dependency eliminated.

auth-service rate_limited_per_min steps to 451.86 avg (max 902.06), ~450x baseline; api-gateway error_rate jumps to 4.78 avg and p99 to 3952.31ms — one bucket after the gateway's own request step, mirroring auth-service.
WARN 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=...)' first appears on auth-service, with accept-queue backlog up to 98763 — pool exhausted before 503s begin.
auth-service error_rate jumps to 14.02%; latency plateau ~3.7-3.9s begins and is sustained through 08:55Z.
First app-level 503: 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)' — admission control rejecting connections.
auth-service logs 'autoscaler: desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' — capacity ceiling reached, autoscaling blocked.
api-gateway request_rate reaches plateau avg 4790.49 (max 4859.74), ~3.9-4.1x pre-onset, held through 07:10Z; auth-service 1749.75 req/s (~3.8x). Multipliers match within noise.
Incident INC-008 reported by on-call SRE: login latency ~4s and 503s; reporter suspected a bcrypt regression as in HIST-101.

Other gateway upstreams confirmed flat across 06:40-07:10Z (portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service); only auth-service moved. Gateway itself flat on CPU/memory, 0 restarts, 0 ERROR logs.
Last sampled bucket: auth-service p99 still ~3.7-3.9s and error_rate ~13.6-14.3% — degradation ongoing at latest data.

recommended_actions.action: Relieve auth-service capacity immediately: raise the auth-service maxReplicas from 8 (e.g. to 14, matching the autoscaler's desired count) and/or increase the fixed 64-thread worker pool size, then confirm replicas actually scale out.
recommended_actions.rationale: F4 shows the autoscaler wanted 14 replicas but was capped at maxReplicas=8 while the pool sat at 64/64 with a ~98k accept-queue backlog; F42 shows the pool is process-wide. This is the direct binding constraint and the fastest mitigation.

recommended_actions.action: Absorb or throttle the external login demand at api-gateway: apply a rate limit / quota on the /v1/auth/login path (or shed load at the edge) while auth-service is over capacity, so admission control stops returning 503s.
recommended_actions.rationale: F39 shows ~450x admission-rejected login requests and F3/F41 show login-path 'accept queue full' 503s; the surge originates as external offered load arriving through the gateway (F24, F36), which is an unsaturated pass-through (F27, F29).

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT roll back or hunt for an auth-service release as the fix. Explicitly verify in the release record that no auth-service deploy occurred in 01:00-09:00Z before escalating a rollback, and stand down the HIST-101 bcrypt theory.
recommended_actions.rationale: F7, F13, F30 and F32 show zero auth-service deployments and no login-path config change across 01:00-09:00Z; the only config change is a 03:40Z log-verbosity edit (F8/F31). A rollback would misdirect the fix and waste the mitigation window.

recommended_actions.action: Identify and quantify the demand generator (client release, retry storm, marketing/traffic event, or bot/malicious client) by inspecting client-side telemetry, upstream partner traffic, and per-client request distributions over 06:45-07:15Z; confirm whether the surge persists or self-resolves.
recommended_actions.rationale: The origin of the ~3.9x offered-load step (F6, F24) is unidentified; without this, any capacity change may be sized wrong, and the demand may re-saturate auth-service after the immediate relief.

recommended_actions.action: Restore and confirm service health after mitigation: verify auth-service p99 returns to ~88-92ms baseline and error_rate to ~0.2%, worker pool drops below 64/64, accept-queue backlog clears, rate_limited_per_min returns to ~1-2/min, and gateway p99/error_rate normalize.
recommended_actions.rationale: F1, F2, F3, F4, F39 define the pre-onset baseline and the saturation signature; these are the observable success criteria for the mitigation.

recommended_actions.action: Instrument the missing dimensions that blocked per-route attribution: add a route/path label to auth-service and api-gateway request_rate, error_rate and latency metrics (and a login-route 503 counter), and expose a latency metric on redis-cache.
recommended_actions.rationale: F34, F35, F40 and F22 document that no per-route or per-path dimension exists and redis exposes no latency metric; this was the single unresolvable detail that capped confidence in this investigation and would let future incidents discriminate load surge from per-route cost changes route-by-route.

recommended_actions.action: Capacity-plan auth-service against peak offered load: set alerting on worker-pool saturation (active/active=64/64), accept-queue depth, and autoscaler desired-vs-max replicas so the maxReplicas ceiling and pool sizing are validated against realistic login burst profiles, not just steady-state ~400 req/s.
recommended_actions.rationale: F4 shows the capacity ceiling was silently binding (desired 14 vs max 8) and F5/F6 show a ~3.9x burst fully saturated the service; proactive detection would have caught the ceiling before 503s began at 06:55:42Z.

data_gaps: No per-route (/v1/auth/login vs /verify vs /refresh) metrics exist on any service (F34, F40), so the exact login-route multiplier could not be measured; the login-vs-other split is only inferred from per-service request_rate deltas. This is the single most important limit on confidence and is why it is capped at 0.70.

The gateway request_rate rose to ~4.8-5.0k req/s while auth-service rose only to ~1.45-1.54k req/s (~3.2x difference), with the gateway's pre-onset baseline ~1230 req/s vs auth-service ~400 req/s; the source of the extra gateway volume (other routes vs fan-out) is unresolved (F38).

Blast radius on the API gateway and other services consuming /v1/auth/login is unconfirmed: a query for 'gateway-service' logs failed as an invalid service name (correct name api-gateway) and no log/metric queries succeeded for order-service, portfolio-service, or other login-path consumers.
kyc-provider is external with has_telemetry:false and no DNS/network component appears as a node, so external auth-path latency or DNS/network contributors cannot be assessed.

redis-cache exposes no latency and no request_rate/keyspace metric, and memory_pct and request_rate queries failed (timeout / 503), so cache-side latency and maxmemory proximity cannot be measured directly; the rejection of the cache hypothesis rests on hit_ratio/evictions/clients/cpu being at baseline rather than on measured cache latency (F22).

The auth-service ERROR log sweep was truncated (104 matched, 40 returned) and two auth-service log queries failed (timeout, 503), so it cannot be stated with certainty that /v1/auth/verify or /v1/auth/refresh produce zero errors, though they were absent from the returned sample and the 32-entry WARN stream (F41, F42).
A historical-incident search for a traffic-surge/load-spike precedent timed out, so only the bcrypt precedent (HIST-101) was available for comparison.

Bucket-level correlation is the finest granularity available; a sub-minute config change inside the 06:50Z bucket would be invisible, and the 00:00-01:00Z hour has no deployment sweep (though it is >5h before onset).
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Discovery of an auth-service deployment, release, or sub-bucket config/feature-flag change touching the login path in the 06:30-06:50Z pre-onset interval (e.g. a bcrypt cost or hashing-work change), which would restore H2. The current continuous change record (F7, F13, F14, F30, F31, F32) found none.

Per-route measurement showing the login-route request multiplier was materially smaller than ~3.9x — e.g. a large non-login surge dominating, or login volume flat while auth-service CPU and latency still jumped — which would favour a per-request cost/capacity change over pure external demand.

Evidence that non-login routes (/v1/auth/verify, /v1/auth/refresh, token issuance) remained healthy at baseline p99 and error rate while only login degraded, which would contradict the route-agnostic process-wide pool saturation picture and point to a login-specific per-request change (H2).

Direct measurement of redis-cache latency or memory utilisation at onset showing a slowdown or maxmemory pressure, which would revive the shared-dependency hypothesis (H3) that F18-F23 currently exclude.

Evidence that auth-service was actually blocked waiting on a downstream (kyc-provider, user-db) rather than CPU-bound — e.g. kyc/user-db latency spikes at 06:50Z — which would overturn the CPU-pinned self-saturation mechanism (H1) in favour of a dependency-stall hypothesis (H4).

Proof that the gateway's ~3.9x request step was a gateway-local event (e.g. a proxy retry or amplification mechanism) rather than pass-through external demand, which would make the gateway a distinct origin (H5) requiring a different fix.

Other gateway upstreams were FLAT across 06:40-07:10Z, so they contribute ~0 to the step-up: portfolio-service 559.17 (06:40Z) -> 560.88 (07:10Z); pricing-engine 640.15 -> 619.94; market-data-service 935.75 -> 967.77. Only auth-service moved.

Fraction/multiplier attribution (inference from the per-service proxy): the gateway rose ~4.1x (1227.99->4990.58) while auth-service rose ~3.8x (386.14->1469.29); their multipliers MATCH within measurement noise. In absolute req/s the auth-service delta (+~1083 req/s) is ~29% of the gateway delta (+~3762 req/s), but the gateway's pre-onset baseline (~1228 req/s) already contained ~386 req/s of auth traffic plus ~386 req/s of other traffic growing in step, so the login-route multiplier (~3.9x) equals the gateway multiplier — consistent with a genuine login-demand surge, not a small login surge amplified by per-request cost/capacity change.

There is no per-route latency or per-route error metric, so the p99/503 elevation cannot be split by /v1/auth/login vs /v1/auth/verify vs /v1/auth/refresh from metrics.

findings.statement: The WARN saturation stream is likewise route-agnostic: pattern 'worker pool saturated (active=<n>/<n>, queue=<n>)' — 32 WARN entries, active=64/64 with queue depths e.g. 39035, 98763, 62284 — first seen 06:54:53Z. The pool is a single process-wide 64-thread pool shared by ALL auth-service routes; the log shows the saturation event itself, not a per-route breakdown.

Aggregate auth-service signals all step at the same 06:49–06:54Z bucket: latency_p99_ms jumps from 91.36 (06:48Z) to 3752.4 (06:54Z) and holds ~3748-3934ms; error_rate from 0.19 (06:48Z) to 11.72 (06:54Z) then ~13.7-14.2%; request_rate from 395.18 (06:42Z) to 1512.39 (06:56Z) ~3.8x; rate_limited_per_min from ~1.8 baseline to 886.18 (06:56Z). This is a whole-service step, not a route-partitioned one.

Because the saturation is expressed at the shared process-wide resource layer (worker pool 64/64 active with a large accept-queue backlog, aggregate CPU/request-rate/rate-limit all stepping together), the degradation mechanism — admission control rejecting connections ahead of routing — is inherently route-agnostic. Login is simply the dominant/first-hit path in the error stream; this is consistent with H1/H5 all-route capacity exhaustion and does NOT provide the login-only isolation that H2 (bcrypt per-request) would require.
